newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico Congress blasts U.S. over drug certification.
newsitem.headline: Mexico Congress blasts U.S. over drug certification.

text.p: Mexican congressmen blasted the United States on Wednesday for grading other countries' anti-narcotics efforts as the political temperature in Mexico rose ahead of Washington's annual announcement on the subject.

One Mexican ruling party senator, Amador Rodriguez Lopez, even accused the American government of colluding with organised crime because of what he termed its failure to attack drug cartels operating in the United States.
"They can't control it because of the corruption which exists among U.S. officials, at all levels, with organised crime in the United States," Rodriguez told reporters.

The U.S. government was expected to announce by the weekend its annual review of which drug-producing or trafficking countries it deemed to have performed adequately in the drug war. Failure to win "certification," as the process is called, can mean economic sanctions.
The process is detested in Latin America, where governments and business leaders say it is an unfair imposition that fails to recognise that the United States is the world's biggest drug market.
Congressmen from Mexico's four main political parties united to sign a statement attacking the process on Wednesday.

"We reiterate our condemnation of any purported process of certification since this is a unilateral act which violates the international order openly and which aims to damage our self-determination and sovereign responsibility to confront drug trafficking", the statement said.

However, opposition party deputies refused to agree to a request from the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) to include in the joint statement a condemnation of a New York Times article last Sunday linking two Mexican state governors to drug traffickers, a deputy said.

"This point had to be modified because the PRI wanted to elevate the New York Times story into an attack on Mexico and its institutions ... something which we didn't agree with," opposition deputy Cuauhtemoc Sandoval told reporters.
Pedro Etienne, parliamentary floor leader for the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), also accused U.S. authorities of turning a blind eye to drug corruption.
